concept.name: Earnings trading
concept.definition: Trading equity positions around quarterly earnings announcements to exploit the announcement-day volatility and the post-announcement price drift documented in the accounting literature. Implementations range from intraday reaction trades to holding surprise winners and losers for the multi-week drift.
concept.intuition: Earnings are scheduled surprises: prices jump at the print and then, on average, keep crawling in the direction of the surprise for weeks, as if the market digests the news only gradually.
concept.mechanics: Screen for upcoming reports, estimate the surprise (actual versus consensus), and trade the direction of the surprise or the subsequent drift. Bernard and Thomas (1989) document post-earnings-announcement drift: abnormal returns continue in the direction of the surprise for roughly 60 days, a pattern they find consistent with delayed price response rather than risk mismeasurement.
concept.formula: Surprise proxies include SUE = (EPS_actual - EPS_expected) / sigma(forecast errors); portfolios sorted on SUE show drift in cumulative abnormal returns over the following quarter.
concept.failure_modes: Announcement windows concentrate gap risk - positions held through the print face binary moves that jump stops - and crowding plus post-publication decay of the drift anomaly compress the available edge.
concept.misconceptions: That earnings trading is just guessing the number; systematic versions trade the market's reaction function (surprise to drift), not the fundamental outcome itself.
concept.example: A stock reports EPS 15% above consensus and gaps up 6% at the open; a drift-following position held for the following weeks targets the continuation documented beyond the initial jump.

citations.source: Bernard & Thomas, 'Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift: Delayed Price Response or Risk Premium?', Journal of Accounting Research 27 (1989), 1-36 (EconPapers record)
